You can use adjectives to make comparisons or to describe something with a highly developed quality.

Short Adjectives:

For both the comparative and the superlative form in short adjectives you keep the adjective in its original form with little changes at the end. In the case of the comparative form, you need to add er at the end to make the comparative form. To make the superlative form, you add the article the before the adjective and -est at the end.

There are a few rules, however, that you have to keep in mind. Take a look at the following chart to learn them in more detail:
PCX was used in the past, but it isn't the most popular format anymore.
The best I can do is to use a lossless format. To publish online, I'll use JPG, which is the most convenient and compatible.

Examples:
Designers use heavier formats than regular consumers.
The greatest graphic formats offer a lot of details and accuracy.

Long Adjectives:

To make the comparative form of long adjectives (adjectives with two or more syllables) all you have to do is add the word more:

Some graphic formats are more flexible than others.

For the superlative form, you need to use the article the and the word most before the adjective:

The most useful formats are quite easy to use.

Remember that adjectives ending with –ing or –ed follow the same rules long adjectives do in both their comparative and superlative form:

Learning how to use these tools is more boring than I expected.
The most advanced editing tools require a lot of resources.
You can use verb to be in past and past participles to talk about a noun or object and an action that affected it.
Remember that verb to be has two forms in past, which are was and were. They are used like this:
PCX was used in the past, but it isn't the most popular format anymore.
It was replaced by the TIFF format which is more modern.

Tom: So, Sean, have you decided what format you're going to use yet?
Sean: Yes, I read about the different formats that I can use and I found that they vary in the use of colors and pixels. I found JPG, PCX and TIFF. They were described in detail on this page a friend recommended me. It has great references.
Tom: I don't know anything about those. I guess they're the least common ones, right?
Sean: Yes. PCX was used in the past, but it isn't the most popular format anymore. It was replaced by the TIFF format which is more modern, but it also has more compatibility issues.

Tom: Well, which one of them is the most common one?
Sean: None of them. Although PCX was used in the early days of computing, it is not so common anymore. TIFF, which stands for Tagged Image File Format, is common among graphic artists and in publishing. This format is still supported by many graphic applications, especially for design layouts or even word-processing.
Tom: So, are you going to use it?
Sean: I don't think so, I think that JPG is the best format I can use for my photos.
Tom: That's great! I know JPG. It's one of the most common graphic formats. Does it have any downsides?

Sean: I read that JPG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group. It's more versatile than the other formats, but it's lossy. This means that it tends to degrade over time due to compression. Lossless versions were developed, but they weren't widely adopted by users.
Tom: Almost all digital cameras use that format and the files don't take much space. What are you going to do, then?
Sean: The best I can do is to use a lossless format. To publish online, I'll use JPG, which is the most convenient and compatible.
